content: Neurosyphilis is an infection of the central nervous system caused by Treponema pallidum, a spirochete bacterium capable of infecting various organs and tissues in the body. This condition represents a tertiary stage of syphilis and can lead to significant neurological complications. The standard first-line treatment for neurosyphilis is aqueous crystalline penicillin. However, alternative antibiotic regimens may be necessary for patients with penicillin allergies. The objective of this study was to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and safety of different antibiotic therapies for adults with neurosyphilis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Library, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and others, up to April 2019. Additionally, proceedings from eight medical congresses over the past decade were reviewed, and trial authors were contacted for supplementary information. The study included randomized clinical trials involving adults with confirmed diagnoses of neurosyphilis, including those who were HIV-positive. The trials compared various antibiotic regimens in terms of concentration, dosage, frequency, and duration. One trial was identified that met the inclusion criteria. This trial involved 36 participants, primarily men, with a median age of 34 years. All participants had syphilis and were HIV-positive. The trial compared two antibiotic regimens: ceftriaxone (2 g daily for 10 days) in 18 participants versus penicillin G (4 million units intravenously every 4 hours for 10 days) in another 18 participants. The trial was funded by a pharmaceutical company and reported incomplete and inconclusive results. In terms of serological cure, 3 out of 18 participants (16%) treated with ceftriaxone achieved this outcome, compared to 2 out of 18 participants (11%) treated with penicillin G (risk ratio [RR] 1.50; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.28 to 7.93). For clinical cure, 8 out of 18 participants (44%) receiving ceftriaxone achieved this outcome, compared to 2 out of 18 participants (18%) receiving penicillin G (RR 4.00; 95% CI: 0.98 to 16.30). However, the evidence was of very low quality, and the small sample size made it impossible to draw definitive conclusions about the comparative effectiveness of these treatments. Although more participants treated with ceftriaxone appeared to achieve serological and clinical cures compared to those treated with penicillin G, the evidence was insufficient to determine whether there was a true difference between the two treatments. The trial did not assess important outcomes such as recurrence of neurosyphilis, time to recovery, or quality of life. Adverse events were reported as symptoms and signs during follow-up, rather than being systematically evaluated. The trial had several methodological limitations, including unclear risk of bias for random sequence generation, allocation, and blinding of participants. There was a high risk of bias due to incomplete outcome data, potential conflicts of interest (funding bias), and the absence of a sample size calculation. As a result, the quality of evidence was rated as very low. The authors concluded that due to the low quality and insufficient evidence, it is not possible to determine whether ceftriaxone is more effective or safer than penicillin G for treating neurosyphilis. Furthermore, the benefits of ceftriaxone for individuals without HIV and neurosyphilis remain unknown, as does its safety profile. These findings should be interpreted with caution. This conclusion does not imply that antibiotics should not be used to treat neurosyphilis. Instead, it highlights the need for well-designed, adequately powered clinical trials. Future studies should adhere to the Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials (SPIRIT) guidelines and the CONSORT statement for reporting. Additionally, outcomes should be patient-centered, following the recommendations of the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute (PCORI).
